about.title: Foster City Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Foster City's mix of office parks, retail corridors, and logistics routes near SR-92 and E Hillsdale Boulevard means workplace injuries here take many forms — from warehouse falls to vehicle collisions suffered while working. San Mateo County's 2025 figures show 107 injury collisions and 139 people injured citywide, a reminder that some of these incidents happen to people simply doing their jobs on the road. In California, workers' compensation is typically the only path against your employer, but that doesn't mean it's the end of the story. If a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or another driver contributed to your injury, you may have a separate claim worth exploring. LawProactive doesn't practice law or promise results — we simply connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney familiar with both the workers' comp system and third-party claims, so you can understand your options with clearer eyes.

whyChoose.title: Why Foster City Workers Use LawProactive

items.title: Understanding the 30-Day Reporting Window
items.desc: California requires injured employees to report a workplace injury to their employer within 30 days. Missing that window can complicate a claim, so getting guidance early matters.

items.title: Spotting Third-Party Liability
items.desc: Workers' comp usually bars claims against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker on a Foster City job site may still be liable separately. An independent attorney can help identify whether that applies to your situation.

items.title: Protection Against Retaliation
items.desc: California law makes it illegal for an employer to retaliate against you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. Knowing this protection exists can make it easier to come forward.

items.question: Can I file a claim if my injury happened while driving for work near SR-92 or Foster City Boulevard?
items.answer: Possibly. If another driver caused the collision while you were performing work duties, you may have both a workers' comp claim and a separate third-party claim against that driver. An independent attorney can look at the specifics of the crash and your job duties to sort out which claims apply.

items.question: Does workers' compensation cover all my losses?
items.answer: Workers' comp generally covers medical treatment and a portion of lost wages, but it typically doesn't cover full pain and suffering damages. If a third party contributed to your injury, a separate claim might address losses that workers' comp doesn't reach.

items.question: What if my employer discourages me from reporting the injury?
items.answer: Retaliation for reporting a workplace injury is illegal under California law, regardless of how an employer reacts. If you're facing pressure or pushback, it's worth speaking with an independent attorney about your rights and the proper reporting steps.
